title: Aldol addition: enolate + aldehyde → β-hydroxy aldehyde
why: Hydroxide removes an α-H to make an enolate. Its α-carbon then runs pattern A on a second aldehyde: nucleophilic addition to the C=O carbon. Protonating the alkoxide gives a β-hydroxy aldehyde.

traps.explains: That's the aldol condensation product. Losing water to form the C=C needs heat; at low temperature the reaction stops at the β-hydroxy aldehyde.
The new C–C bond joins the α-carbon of one aldehyde to the carbonyl carbon of the other, so the OH ends up on the β-carbon, not the α-carbon.
Hydroxide isn't a reducing agent. The aldehyde C=O survives; only the attacked C=O becomes an alcohol.

review: Check the conditions (NaOH, 5 °C = addition; heat = condensation) follow the usual textbook split.

title: Acid-catalysed α-bromination → α-bromo ketone
why: Acid catalyses formation of the enol, whose α-carbon attacks Br2. Once one Br is on, the C=O is less basic, so enol formation slows and the reaction stops at the mono-bromo ketone (in base, every α-H is replaced).

traps.explains: Polyhalogenation happens in base, where each Br makes the next α-H more acidic. In acid, the reaction stops after one Br.
Brominating the benzene ring (EAS) needs a Lewis acid like FeBr3. Here the enol's α-carbon is the nucleophile.
Cleaving off the methyl as a haloform needs base (NaOH) and excess halogen. Acid conditions give the α-bromo ketone.

title: Haloform: methyl ketone + I2/NaOH → carboxylic acid + CHI3
why: In base each α-iodination makes the remaining α-H's more acidic, so all three H's on the methyl are replaced. Hydroxide then does pattern B on the C=O with CI3⁻ as the leaving group, giving a carboxylate (an acid after workup) and yellow iodoform, CHI3.

traps.explains: Stopping at one halogen is the acid-catalysed result. In base, halogenation speeds up after each step, so all three α-H's are replaced.
The triiodo ketone is an intermediate: hydroxide attacks its C=O and kicks out CI3⁻ as a leaving group.
The CH3 carbon leaves as CHI3, so the acid keeps the carbonyl carbon and loses one carbon overall.

review: Key step shown is hydroxide adding to the C=O of the CI3 ketone (the C–C bond breaks in the next step, when the tetrahedral intermediate expels CI3⁻). Check this is the step you want drilled.

title: Kinetic enolate (LDA, −78 °C) + CH3I → less substituted α-carbon
why: LDA is a strong, bulky base: at −78 °C it removes the most accessible α-H (on the CH2 side) fast and irreversibly, giving the kinetic (less substituted) enolate. Its α-carbon then does SN2 on CH3I, giving 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone.

traps.explains: That's the thermodynamic result (alkylation at the more substituted α-carbon), from an equilibrating base such as NaOEt at room temperature. Cold, bulky LDA deprotonates the less hindered side.
Enolates alkylate on carbon with alkyl halides like CH3I. The O-methyl enol ether is not the main product.
CH3I is an electrophile, not a carbon nucleophile, so nothing adds to the C=O. The enolate carbon attacks the CH3 of CH3I.

distractors.explains: An equilibrating base forms the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate, giving 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone.
One alkylation of cyclohexanone puts on only one methyl, giving 2-methylcyclohexanone.

title: Thermodynamic enolate + CH3I → more substituted α-carbon
why: A weaker base at room temperature deprotonates reversibly, so the enolates equilibrate and the more substituted (more stable) C=C enolate wins. Its α-carbon does SN2 on CH3I, putting the second methyl on the carbon that already has one.

traps.explains: That's the kinetic product, from LDA at −78 °C. Reversible, room-temperature conditions favour the more substituted enolate.
Enolates alkylate on carbon with CH3I; the O-methyl enol ether is not the main product.
The new bond forms at the ring α-carbon, not on the existing methyl group. Those methyl H's are not α to the C=O.

distractors.explains: Cold, bulky LDA forms the less substituted (kinetic) enolate, giving 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone.
A Grignard adds to the C=O, giving 1,2-dimethylcyclohexanol, not an α-alkylated ketone.

review: Textbooks vary on how cleanly thermodynamic-enolate alkylation works (with NaOEt/EtOH there is also polyalkylation and some 2,6-product). Check the conditions shown (NaOEt, EtOH, 25 °C; NaH accepted as an alias) match the course's convention.

title: Enolate alkylation: ketone + LDA, then 1° alkyl halide
why: LDA converts all of the ketone to its enolate, so there is no leftover ketone to self-condense. The enolate α-carbon then does SN2 on the unhindered 1° alkyl bromide, making a new C–C bond next to the C=O.

traps.explains: That's what a propyl Grignard would give. Here the ketone is the nucleophile (as its enolate) and the alkyl halide is the electrophile.
Enolates alkylate on carbon with alkyl halides; the propyl enol ether (O-alkylation) is not the main product.
One equivalent of LDA and alkyl halide gives one alkylation. Dialkylation would need a second round of base and RX.

distractors.explains: A Grignard adds to the C=O, giving 1-propylcyclohexanol, not an α-alkylated ketone.
OH⁻ is a terrible leaving group, so the alcohol can't be attacked; it just protonates the enolate back to cyclohexanone.

title: Aldol condensation (heat) → α,β-unsaturated aldehyde
why: Enolate + pattern A: the enolate α-carbon adds to the C=O carbon of a second propanal, giving a β-hydroxy aldehyde. With heat, base removes the now doubly-activated α-H and expels OH⁻ (E1cB), giving the conjugated C=C: 2-methylpent-2-enal.

traps.explains: That's the aldol addition product. With heat, the β-hydroxy aldehyde loses water to give the conjugated enal.
The new C–C bond is made by the α-carbon (the CH2 next to C=O), so the product carries a methyl branch at C2. A straight chain would need the CH3 end to be nucleophilic.
That's a Claisen-type (pattern B) product. An aldehyde has no leaving group, so the alkoxide stays on and becomes OH, then leaves as water.

distractors.explains: Cold conditions stop at the aldol addition product (the β-hydroxy aldehyde); no water is lost.
An ester does a Claisen condensation, giving a β-keto ester, not an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde.

title: Crossed aldol (Claisen–Schmidt): ketone + benzaldehyde → enone
why: Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile, and as an aldehyde it is a better one than the ketone. Enolate + pattern A on the aldehyde C=O, then loss of water gives the C=C conjugated with both the ring and the C=O (a chalcone).

traps.explains: That's the aldol addition product. Losing water here gives a C=C conjugated with both the ring and the C=O, so dehydration goes easily.
That's acetophenone condensing with itself. Benzaldehyde's C=O is the more reactive electrophile, so the crossed product wins.
Nothing here reduces the C=C. The dehydration step leaves the conjugated alkene in the product.

distractors.explains: Acetaldehyde's enolate gives cinnamaldehyde (PhCH=CHCHO), an aldehyde, not the phenyl ketone.
A Grignard adds twice to an acid chloride, giving a tertiary alcohol, not the ketone.

title: Intramolecular aldol: 2,5-hexanedione → cyclopentenone
why: Enolate + pattern A, inside one molecule: the enolate of a terminal CH3 attacks the other C=O, closing a strain-free five-membered ring. Dehydration with heat gives the conjugated enone, 3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one.

traps.explains: That's the aldol addition product. With heat it loses water to give the conjugated cyclopentenone.
Count the atoms: 2,5-hexanedione closes a five-membered ring. The cyclohexenone comes from 2,6-heptanedione.
The methyl ends up on the β-carbon (the former C=O carbon that was attacked), not on the α-carbon next to the remaining C=O.

distractors.explains: 2,6-Heptanedione closes a six-membered ring, giving 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one.
The cuprate adds 1,4, giving 3-methylcyclopentanone; the C=C is gone.

title: Claisen condensation: 2 ethyl acetate → β-keto ester
why: Enolate + pattern B: the ester enolate adds to a second ester's C=O, and because esters have a leaving group the tetrahedral intermediate kicks out EtO⁻ instead of becoming an alcohol (contrast aldol = enolate + pattern A). Ethoxide then deprotonates the acidic β-keto ester, which drives the reaction; H3O+ workup gives ethyl acetoacetate.

traps.explains: That's aldol thinking (pattern A). An ester's tetrahedral intermediate expels EtO⁻ and re-forms the C=O, so the product is a ketone.
Losing CO2 needs the ester hydrolysed and then heat (as in the acetoacetic ester synthesis). Mild H3O+ workup only protonates the enolate.
The workup is mild acid at room temperature, so the ethyl ester survives. Only the enolate is protonated.

distractors.explains: Hydroxide saponifies the ester to acetic acid; no C–C bond forms.
A Grignard adds twice to the ester, giving 2-methyl-2-propanol.

title: Dieckmann: diethyl hexanedioate → cyclic β-keto ester
why: A Dieckmann is an intramolecular Claisen (enolate + pattern B): the enolate α to one ester attacks the other ester's C=O, and EtO⁻ leaves, closing a five-membered ring. Deprotonation of the cyclic β-keto ester drives it; H3O+ workup gives ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate.

traps.explains: Count the ring: the α-carbon and the other C=O carbon of a hexanedioate are five atoms apart, so a five-membered ring forms. The cyclohexanone comes from the heptanedioate.
Losing the ester as CO2 needs hydrolysis and heat. Mild H3O+ workup leaves the β-keto ester intact.
The enolate carbon bonds directly to the other C=O, so the ester ends up on the carbon between the two carbonyls (a β-keto ester), not one carbon further away.

distractors.explains: Diethyl heptanedioate closes a six-membered ring, giving ethyl 2-oxocyclohexanecarboxylate.
Hydroxide saponifies both esters, giving hexanedioic (adipic) acid; no ring forms.

title: Crossed Claisen: ketone + non-enolizable ester → 1,3-diketone
why: Ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile. The acetone enolate does pattern B on the ester C=O and EtO⁻ leaves; deprotonation of the very acidic 1,3-diketone pulls the reaction through, and workup gives 1-phenylbutane-1,3-dione.

traps.explains: That's aldol (pattern A) thinking. An ester has a leaving group, so the tetrahedral intermediate expels EtO⁻ and a ketone forms.
That's acetone condensing with itself. The self-aldol is reversible, while the 1,3-diketone is trapped as its stable enolate, so the crossed Claisen product wins.
The bond forms from acetone's α-carbon, not its C=O carbon, so a CH2 sits between the two C=O groups (a 1,3-, not a 1,2-dicarbonyl).

distractors.explains: With an aldehyde this is an aldol condensation, giving the enone PhCH=CHCOCH3, not a 1,3-diketone.
A Grignard adds twice to the ester, giving 2-phenyl-2-propanol.

review: The 1,3-diketone is drawn as the diketo form; in reality 1-phenylbutane-1,3-dione exists largely as its enol tautomer. Acetone self-aldol is a competing side reaction (the self-condensation trap explains why the crossed product dominates). Check the substrate pair is acceptable or swap to ethyl benzoate + ethyl acetate.

title: Michael addition: malonate enolate + enone → 1,5-dicarbonyl
why: Enolate + pattern C: the stabilized (soft) malonate enolate adds 1,4 to the β-carbon of the enone rather than to its C=O. Protonation of the new enolate on workup gives a 1,5-dicarbonyl compound.

traps.explains: That's 1,2-addition to the C=O, the hard-nucleophile result. A stabilized malonate enolate is soft and adds 1,4.
The nucleophile bonds to the β-carbon (the CH2 end of the C=C), not the α-carbon next to the C=O.
Hydrolysis and loss of CO2 need H3O+ with heat. A mild workup leaves both esters in place.

distractors.explains: Hot aqueous acid also hydrolyses the esters and decarboxylates, giving 5-oxohexanoic acid.
Michael addition to crotonaldehyde gives a branched aldehyde, (EtO2C)2CH–CH(CH3)–CH2–CHO, not the methyl ketone.

title: Robinson annulation: cyclohexanone + MVK → bicyclic enone
why: Robinson annulation = Michael (enolate + pattern C) then intramolecular aldol condensation (enolate + pattern A). The key step drilled is the Michael: the cyclohexanone enolate adds 1,4 to MVK; then the methyl ketone's enolate closes a six-membered ring onto the ring C=O, and dehydration gives the conjugated bicyclic enone.

traps.explains: That's only the Michael adduct. With base and heat it goes on to an intramolecular aldol condensation that closes the second ring.
That's the aldol addition product (β-hydroxy ketone). Heat drives the loss of water to the conjugated enone.
The enolate adds 1,4 to the β-carbon of MVK, not 1,2 to its C=O.

distractors.explains: Starting from cyclopentanone gives the 5,6-fused enone (a hexahydroindenone), one ring carbon short.
2-Methylcyclohexanone gives the octalone with an extra angular methyl at the ring fusion.

review: Key step is the Michael step only (stated in why). Check the conditions shown (NaOEt, EtOH, heat; one pot) match the course convention; some texts write 1. NaOEt, 2. heat or use KOH/MeOH.

title: Malonic ester synthesis → carboxylic acid
why: Ethoxide removes the acidic H between the two esters, and that enolate's α-carbon does SN2 on the 1° alkyl bromide. Hot aqueous acid then hydrolyses both esters and the resulting malonic acid loses CO2, leaving RCH2COOH (here butanoic acid).

traps.explains: Heat makes the 1,3-diacid lose CO2. Only one COOH stays.
One equivalent of base and alkyl halide gives one alkylation. A second ethyl would need a second round of NaOEt and EtBr.
Count carbons: the malonate CH2 and one COOH stay, and the ethyl group is added to that CH2, so the acid has four carbons.

distractors.explains: The acetoacetic ester synthesis gives a methyl ketone (2-pentanone), not a carboxylic acid.
A propyl group gives one carbon too many: pentanoic acid.

title: Acetoacetic ester synthesis → methyl ketone
why: Ethoxide removes the acidic H between the ketone and ester C=O, and the enolate's α-carbon does SN2 on the alkyl bromide. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyses the ester to a β-keto acid, which loses CO2, so the product is a methyl ketone: CH3CO–CH2–R (here 2-pentanone).

traps.explains: That's the alkylated β-keto ester before step 3. Hot H3O+ hydrolyses the ester and the β-keto acid loses CO2.
That's the malonic ester result. Starting from ethyl acetoacetate, the acetyl group stays, giving a methyl ketone.
One equivalent of base and EtBr adds one ethyl. Dialkylation needs a second round of NaOEt and RX.

distractors.explains: The malonic ester synthesis gives a carboxylic acid (butanoic acid), not a methyl ketone.
A propyl group gives 2-hexanone, one carbon too many.

title: Decarboxylation of a β-keto acid (heat) → ketone + CO2
why: A β-keto acid loses CO2 through a cyclic six-membered transition state: the acid H moves to the ketone O while the C–C bond to the COOH breaks, giving CO2 and an enol. The enol then tautomerizes to the ketone.

traps.explains: The carbon that leaves is the COOH carbon, as CO2. The ring ketone stays.
The enol is the first product, but it tautomerizes to the much more stable keto form.
Only the COOH carbon is lost; the six-membered ring stays intact.

review: Key-step arrows are simplified: the validator can't reference explicit H atoms, so the O–H → ketone-O proton transfer of the cyclic TS is drawn as 'O lone pair forms C=O of CO2; C–C bond forms the enol C=C; C=O π goes to the ketone O' (three arrows, no H). nucleophileAtom = the OH oxygen, electrophileAtom = the ketone O that picks up the H. Check this is acceptable.

title: Stork enamine alkylation → α-allyl ketone
why: The ketone and a 2° amine form an enamine, a neutral enolate equivalent: the N lone pair pushes into the C=C, and the α-carbon does SN2 on the reactive allyl bromide. Aqueous acid then hydrolyses the iminium back to the C=O, giving the mono-alkylated ketone without needing a strong base.

traps.explains: That's what an allyl Grignard would do. Here the ketone's α-carbon (via the enamine) is the nucleophile and allyl bromide is the electrophile.
The alkylated iminium can't react again, so the Stork method gives clean mono-alkylation.
Step 3 (H3O+) hydrolyses the iminium/enamine back to the ketone, releasing pyrrolidine.

distractors.explains: A Grignard adds to the C=O, giving 1-allylcyclohexanol, not an α-allyl ketone.
The cuprate adds 1,4, putting the allyl group on the β-carbon: 3-allylcyclohexanone.
